intro/hello: This lecture is about the two ends of a language model: where text goes in, and where text comes out.
intro/vectors: The transformer from the last chapter turns a list of vectors into a list of vectors. But text is not vectors.
intro/tok: So first, a tokenizer cuts the text into pieces from a fixed list, the vocabulary, and replaces each piece with its number in that list.
intro/emb: Then an embedding table turns each id into a vector, simply by looking up one row.
intro/tf: The transformer works on those vectors, and hands back one vector per position.
intro/unemb: At the top, the unembedding turns the last vector into a score for every token in the vocabulary.
intro/next: The best score, or a random draw, is the next token, and decoding turns it back into text.
intro/odd: Of these pieces, the tokenizer is the odd one out. It is not a neural network, and gradient descent never touches it.
intro/leak: It is built once, by counting, then frozen. Yet everything the model reads or writes passes through it.
units/first: The first decision is the unit. The two obvious choices, characters and words, both fail, in instructive ways.
units/chars: Characters, like the character model in the R N N chapter, need a tiny vocabulary, and no word is ever unknown.
units/long: But sequences get long. This one sentence is forty three characters.
units/square: And in a transformer, every token attends to every earlier one, so the work grows with the square of the length.
units/words: Words make sequences short: just seven tokens here.
units/explode: But the vocabulary explodes. Run, runs, running and runner are four unrelated entries, and the list of word forms never ends.
units/unk: Worse, any word missing from the list becomes a single unknown token. Three of these seven words are simply lost.
units/sub: Subwords sit in between. Frequent words get a token of their own, and rare words are spelled out of frequent pieces.
units/pieces: Lighthouses becomes lighthouse, plus an s. Nothing is ever unknown, because the pieces go all the way down to single bytes.
units/dial: So every tokenizer sets one dial. A bigger vocabulary means shorter sequences, and a smaller one means longer sequences.
units/costs: Long sequences cost compute and context. A big vocabulary costs parameters, and data to train every entry.
bpe/name: The most widely used way to choose subwords is byte-pair encoding, or B P E.
bpe/history: It began as a compression trick in nineteen ninety four, came to machine translation in twenty fifteen, and G P T two made it work on raw bytes in twenty nineteen.
bpe/one: The whole algorithm fits in one sentence: find the most frequent pair of neighbors, glue it into a new symbol, and repeat.
bpe/start: Take a tiny text: the hat, the cat, that hat, the bat. As bytes, it is thirty five tokens, each a number below two hundred and fifty six.
bpe/count: Count every pair of neighbors. Ay, then tee, appear together five times, more than any other pair.
bpe/glue: So ay tee becomes token two hundred and fifty six, and every occurrence is replaced. Thirty five tokens become thirty.
bpe/th: Count again. Now tee, aitch, wins with four, and becomes token two hundred and fifty seven.
bpe/the: Then the new token tee aitch, followed by an ee, becomes tee aitch ee, token two hundred and fifty eight.
bpe/on: Each merge adds one entry to the vocabulary and shortens the text. The most frequent strings get glued first.
bpe/cross: Keep going, and merges start to cross spaces and commas: ay tee, comma, space becomes one token.
bpe/end: After eight merges the text is ten tokens long, and no pair occurs twice, so training stops.
bpe/greedy: That is all of training: no gradients, no loss, just counting. The number of merges sets the vocabulary size.
page/real: On a real page of text, B P E rediscovers the structure of the language, with no rules given.
page/story: Here it trains on a short story about a lighthouse keeper: one thousand, five hundred and seventy five bytes.
page/early: The first merges are common pairs, aitch ee and space tee, then space the, with its leading space.
page/words: Soon whole words of the story become single tokens: keeper, night, wind.
page/curve: The blue curve is the text's length, in tokens per byte. It falls fast at first, then slowly.
page/dial: Every merge moves the dial one notch: the vocabulary grows by one, and the text shrinks.
page/end: After a hundred and seventy one merges, no pair occurs twice. The vocabulary is four hundred and twenty seven, and a token averages about three bytes.
page/new: The purple curve is new text in the same style, which training never saw. It falls too.
page/memorize: But the last merges memorize words that occur only twice, like eleven and thousand. In a text about anything else, those slots are wasted.
page/split: Notice that every token stays inside one word. Before counting, the text is split into words, and merges never cross that line.
page/scale: Real tokenizers train on huge, varied text, so every merge earns its slot.
encode/two: Training leaves two things behind: the ordered list of merges, and the bytes behind every id. Together, they are the whole tokenizer.
encode/replay: To encode new text, start from its bytes, and replay the merges in the order they were learned.
encode/oldest: At every step, find the earliest learned merge that applies anywhere, and apply it everywhere.
encode/why: Order matters. Space wrote is glued from space, double-u, ar, oh, and tee ee, so that rule can only fire once both pieces exist.
encode/watch: Watch: the keeper wrote it down. Twenty four bytes become six tokens, one merge at a time.
encode/stop: When no pair in the text was ever learned, encoding stops. Whatever is left is the answer.
encode/decode: Decoding is simpler. Each id stands for fixed bytes: look them up, join them, and read the bytes as text.
encode/space: One surprise. The story always put a space before lighthouse, so space lighthouse is a single token, while lighthouse without the space takes five.
encode/special: Real vocabularies also hold special tokens that no merge can make. G P T two's end of text token marks where one document stops and the next begins.
encode/gpt2: So G P T two's vocabulary of fifty thousand, two hundred and fifty seven is two hundred and fifty six bytes, fifty thousand merges, and that one special token.
bytes/problem: Starting B P E from characters brings the unknown token back. Unicode defines more than a hundred and fifty thousand characters, far too many to list.
bytes/bytes: So G P T two starts one level lower, from bytes. Computers store text as U T F eight, which writes every character as one to four bytes.
bytes/base: A byte has only two hundred and fifty six possible values. Start from those, and every string ever typed can be encoded. No unknown token, ever.
bytes/ascii: English letters take one byte each, exactly as in old ask-ee files.
bytes/two: Accented letters, Greek, and Russian take two bytes per character.
bytes/three: Chinese characters take three bytes, and most emoji take four.
bytes/cost: Here is the catch. Merges follow the text the tokenizer trained on, and ours only ever saw English.
bytes/greek: So the Greek word for good morning, eight letters, stays sixteen tokens: one per byte, two per letter.
bytes/unfair: Real tokenizers trained mostly on English show a milder form of this: other languages pay more tokens for the same meaning.
bytes/fix: Multilingual tokenizers fight back with balanced training text and bigger vocabularies.
quirks/split: Before merging, G P T two cuts text into chunks with a regular expression: runs of letters, runs of digits, and runs of punctuation.
quirks/why: Merges never cross a chunk boundary, so no vocabulary is wasted on pairs like a word plus a full stop.
quirks/space: Each chunk carries at most one leading space. So space the and plain the are different tokens with unrelated ids, and so are capital the and space capital the.
quirks/learn: The model has to learn, from data alone, that all four are the same word.
quirks/letters: And the model never sees letters. Ask how many aitches are in lighthouse, and our tokenizer hands the model a single id: three hundred and sixty six.
quirks/straw: That is why models famously miscounted the ars in strawberry: they see a few tokens, not ten letters.
quirks/numbers: Numbers are worse. G P T two's merges treated digits like letters: common numbers became single tokens, and others split wherever earlier merges fell.
quirks/threes: G P T four's tokenizer instead cuts digits into chunks of at most three, counting from the left.
quirks/align: But then the places stop lining up: four eight two, then one three, against seven seven five, then nine.
quirks/digits: Lama and Lama two split every number into single digits: consistent places, at the price of longer sequences.
quirks/glitch: Last, a token can sit in the vocabulary yet almost never appear in the model's training text. Its embedding barely trains.
quirks/magikarp: The famous case, a username, Solid Gold Magikarp, made G P T three era models produce bizarre replies when asked to repeat it.
embed/ints: After tokenization, the model holds integers, and an integer alone is a poor input: token one thousand is not more than token nine hundred and ninety nine.
embed/table: So the first layer is a lookup table, the embedding matrix E: one row of d learned numbers for each of the V tokens.
embed/row: Token t becomes x, row t of the table.
embed/onehot: In math, the lookup is a one-hot vector, all zeros except a single one at position t, times the matrix.
embed/picks: Every row gets multiplied by zero except row t, so the product is exactly that row.
embed/linear: So the embedding is an ordinary linear layer, and backpropagation trains it like any other weight.
embed/sparse: Its gradient only touches the rows of tokens in the batch. A token that never appears never moves.
embed/learn: What do the rows learn? Nobody tells them, except through the loss.
embed/toy: Here is the smallest language model there is: a two dimensional embedding, one two by two matrix, and an unembedding, trained on a language of fourteen words.
embed/clusters: As it trains, words that are followed by the same things slide together: the with a, the three adjectives, cat with dog.
embed/apart: Bird and fish stay apart, because different verbs follow them.
embed/meaning: With thousands of dimensions instead of two, directions in this space come to line up with meaning.
embed/position: The table cannot know position: a token gets the same row wherever it sits. Order is added separately, as the transformer chapter showed.
unembed/top: At the top of the stack, the transformer hands back one vector, h, for each position.
unembed/scores: To predict the next token, that vector has to become a score for every one of the V tokens.
unembed/matmul: That is one matrix multiply: z equals h times U, where U has d rows and V columns.
unembed/column: Each column of U is an output vector for one token, and that token's score is the dot product of h with its column.
unembed/points: So a token scores high when h points its way. In our tiny model, after cat, h points toward runs and sleeps.
unembed/softmax: A softmax turns the scores into probabilities that add up to one.
unembed/classifier: If this looks familiar, it should. It is the linear softmax classifier from C S two thirty one N, with one class per token.
unembed/gpt2: The last layer of G P T two is a softmax classifier with fifty thousand, two hundred and fifty seven classes.
unembed/steer: Every layer below exists to steer h toward the output vectors of likely next tokens.
unembed/cost: And this layer is not cheap: a d by V multiply at every position.
tying/side: Put the two tables side by side: E has a row for every token, and U a column for every token. Both hold one vector per token, in the same space.
tying/tie: Weight tying uses one matrix for both jobs: U is E, transposed.
tying/who: The original Transformer did this, and so does G P T two.
tying/score: Now the score for token j is how well h lines up with j's own embedding.
tying/saves: It saves a whole table: for G P T two small, thirty eight point six million parameters, almost a third of the model.
tying/rare: It also helps rare tokens. An input row trains only when its token appears, but an output vector trains at every position, since the softmax pushes every wrong token down a little.
tying/share: Tied, those constant nudges train the input vectors of rare tokens too.
tying/cost: The price is a compromise: one vector must say both what a token is, and when it comes next.
tying/scale: How much does vocabulary cost? Each table holds V times d numbers, while each transformer block holds about twelve d squared.
tying/xl: So its share shrinks as models grow: about five percent of G P T two X L, and four percent of a seven billion parameter model with thirty two thousand tokens, even untied.
tying/vocab: That is why vocabularies grew, from fifty thousand tokens in G P T two to around two hundred thousand today: big models can afford them, and shorter sequences pay them back.
outro/tok: A tokenizer cuts text into subword tokens. B P E learns them by counting: merge the most frequent pair, and repeat.
outro/bytes: Starting from the two hundred and fifty six byte values means nothing is ever unknown.
outro/quirks: Its choices explain a lot: spaces glued to words, odd numbers, trouble with spelling, and higher costs for some languages.
outro/emb: The embedding table turns each id into a learned vector.
outro/unemb: The unembedding turns the final vector back into a score per token, a softmax classifier over the vocabulary. Tying makes the two one matrix.
outro/next: Next comes training: how a model learns to predict those next tokens, and how we sample from it.
outro/chapter: In the interactive chapter, you can train B P E with a slider, encode any text, and watch an embedding space form. See you there.
